item.title: The State of Ransomware in Retail (2026)
item.description:
Exploited vulnerabilities hit retail harder than any other sector

Exploited vulnerabilities declined as a technical root cause across all sectors in 2026, but they still started 26% of attacks on retail organizations. That's the highest rate of any sector and well above the 18% cross-sector rate.

Phishing was the top technical root cause for retail at 29%, followed by exploited vulnerabilities (26%) and malicious email (22%).

Identity-based vectors, including malicious email, phishing, compromised credentials, and brute force attacks, initiated 69% of attacks against retail. This was the lowest rate of any sector yet still well above half of respondents. 66% of retail victims said their ransomware attack was also their most significant identity attack, close to the 67% cross-sector rate featured in our State of Identity Security 2026 report earlier in the year.

Known security gaps were retail’s one above-average weakness

38% of retail victims attributed their breach to a known security gap, a weakness they were aware of but had not addressed. That was retail’s most common operational root cause and the only one it cited more often than the 36% cross-sector rate.

Every other operational root cause came in below the cross-sector rate. The report compares each one in detail.

Encryption climbed after two years of decline

62% of attacks on retail succeeded in encrypting data, up from 48% in 2025 and above the 56% cross-sector rate. Attacks that encrypted data and also stole it rose to 19%, up from 14% last year. That second point of leverage weighs heavily on retailers holding customer payment and personal data.

Backups did most of the recovery work: 71% of retail organizations restored data from backups, up from 62% last year and above the 66% cross-sector rate. Far fewer retailers paid the ransom to get their data back than in 2025. The full report shows where retail’s payment rate ranks against other sectors.

Low typical ransoms, with a heavy top end

The median ransom demand for retail was $225,000, the second lowest of any sector and far below the $698,000 cross-sector median. The average (mean) demand was $4.32 million, the highest of any sector. That average does not include outlier ransoms of $40 million or more. These ultra-high ransoms were excluded from the report results to prevent skewing of averages.

The median ransom payment for retail was also low at $57,500, the lowest of any sector and well below the $769,000 cross-sector median.

The report explains what pushed retail’s average demand to the top of the sector rankings and how far retailers negotiated attackers down. 

Recovery got faster, but costs went up

The average (mean) cost to recover from an attack, excluding any ransom paid, rose to $1.76 million from $1.65 million last year. That was slightly above the $1.70 million cross-sector average, which also rose this year.

But on the positive side, retail’s average time to fully recover fell to 2.54 weeks from 3.16 weeks last year. 56% recovered within a week, the highest share in five years of retail data. The rate of 2.54 weeks is also below the 2.80-week cross-sector average, making 2026 a strong year for quick recoveries. 

Defenses saw the attack, but did not stop it

Almost all retail victims of credential-based attacks had MFA enabled (97%), yet more than half still had data encrypted by attackers. Firewalls flagged 59% of attacks before the ransomware deployed, but even with early indicators, victims were encrypted 60% of the time, compared with 50% across all sectors.

Controls in retail are collecting the right signals, but they’re not connecting deeply enough with other tools and responding together. The report contains several key recommendations based on this year’s data, and one of those recommendations is to adopt a defense system posture where identity, email, endpoint, and network controls respond as one.

Read the report

Retail is paying attackers less than any other sector and recovering faster than in any year of our data. But more attacks are reaching encryption, and the cost to recover went up. Closing known security gaps and connecting existing defenses are the highest-leverage places for retailers to invest in.

Download the free report for the full findings, sector comparisons, and recommendations.

item.title: Your training data is boring: Anomaly detection with LLMs
item.description:
Following on from research presented at Black Hat USA 2025, Sophos data scientists Ben Gelman, Tamas Nyiri, and Tibor Kristóf Lányi recently showcased new work on anomaly detection at BSides Las Vegas 2026. As promised, we’re sharing more details of that research (the recording of the talk is also available here).

Supervised classifiers in cybersecurity are often trained on data that doesn't capture the most unusual examples. Benign training sets are dominated by simple, common patterns, while malicious sets reflect known attacks from past investigations. The long tail of unusual files on both sides goes unlabeled.

When these files appear in production, classifiers are more likely to misclassify them, generating false positives that overwhelm SOCs, and false negatives that let threats through.

Traditional approaches to labeling difficult examples rarely scale. Doing it manually is expensive, rule-based collection is too narrow, and anomaly detection alone has historically produced unacceptable false positive rates. But anomaly detection combined with LLMs is excellent at something else: finding and labeling the unusual data that is missing from cybersecurity training sets.

The team developed an automated pipeline that combines anomaly detection and LLMs to augment training data for a suite of cybersecurity models, using complementary anomaly detection methods, viable across feature representations, to surface distinctly unusual data. Then, an LLM classified each anomaly with format-specific prompts calibrated per data type.

Critically, Ben and his colleagues used separate prompts that err toward malicious and benign respectively, achieving high precision on both label types. More specifically, one prompt instructed the LLM to only evaluate the input as benign when it was confident that it was benign; the other prompt instructed the same but with the malicious label. This way, they only accepted the labels when the two LLMs with the two different instructions agreed, otherwise they threw that example away and didn’t use it for training. In practice, this method produced labels with better precision (tested on labeled data). The labeled anomalies augment the training data for cybersecurity classifiers.

The Sophos AI team evaluated their method across three structurally different data types with monthly ingestion scales spanning four orders of magnitude: command lines, HTML, and RTF.

The problem

Every detection team is familiar with the core issue: supervised classifiers are only as good as their training data, and that data is systematically biased. Benign training data comes from sources chosen for labeling confidence.

Known-clean networks, corporate environments without incidents and regex-capturable patterns are obvious choices, but they inherently exclude the long tail of unusual but legitimate data.

Malicious training data is similarly constrained to known attack types from incident investigations. The events that classifiers get wrong in production are precisely the unusual events missing from both sides of the training set.

Using command lines as an example: prior work on anomaly detection for command-line classification has attempted to address labeling oversights by surfacing anomalies as direct alerts. SCADE uses isolation forests and engineered features to flag potentially malicious command lines at scale, but reports false positive rates around 2%. Filar and French discover anomalous parent-child process relationships using tree-based models, reporting similar ~3% false positive rates. Nisslmueller combines explicit command-line featurization with parent-child context for unsupervised LOLBin detection, also landing under 2% FP.

Although these rates sound low, at tens of millions of daily events they still produce overwhelming alert volumes. All three share the fundamental limitation of treating anomaly detection as an end-to-end alerting mechanism.

Ben and team’s approach sidesteps this limitation entirely: anomaly detection surfaces candidates, an LLM labels them, and the labels improve a downstream supervised classifier.

A key takeaway from the team’s work is the prompt strategy for achieving high precision on both malicious and benign labels. A single prompt struggles to simultaneously maintain high precision on both labels. Instead, the team used two separate prompts per file type: one that errs on the side of calling files malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), and another that errs on the side of calling files benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). This allows both label types from anomaly detection to be usable as training data, which was not achievable in prior work that relied on a single labeling pass.

Stand back, we’re doing science

The pipeline for Ben and team’s research was as follows:

  1. Raw production telemetry
  2. Feature extraction
  3. Multi-method anomaly detection
  4. LLM classification
  5. Newly labeled training data from the long tail
  6. Supervised classifier improvement

A key architectural decision was to treat anomaly detection not as the detection system itself, but as a prefilter that surfaces candidates for LLM labeling, which in turn produces training data for a supervised classifier whose precision can be controlled empirically.

Because each anomaly detection method has blind spots – it catches certain types of unusual data and misses others – Sophos AI used three methods (isolation forest, k-means anomaly, and PCA reconstruction error) on different feature representations, producing broader coverage with low overlap between methods.

The team employed several different feature sets, which contributed to data diversity:

  • Hand-crafted features: Catching structural anomalies, such as files with extreme length, abnormal Shannon entropy, rare character distributions. Hand-crafted features included character-level statistics, operator/case proportions, and file-type-specific markers.
  • TF-IDF vectors: To catch content-level outliers, e.g., files whose token distribution didn't match any typical cluster.
  • Binary vocabulary vectors: For the unusual feature correlations, e.g., files with atypical token co-occurrence patterns.

Prompt needed

A single LLM prompt can’t always achieve high precision on both malicious and benign labels simultaneously, especially in cases where the problem itself is inherently ambiguous, such as dual use scripts . For example, if the prompt says, ‘when uncertain, lean toward malicious,’ benign precision is high, but malicious precision suffers and vice versa.

Sophos AI’s solution was to run two separate prompts per file type. One erred towards malicious (producing high-precision benign labels), the other toward benign (producing high-precision malicious labels). Each prompt was calibrated to the file type's specific attack surface.

For example, with HTML, the malicious-leaning prompt defined what normal HTML looks like (JavaScript, forms, analytics) so it didn’t over-flag standard web features. The benign-leaning prompt defined specific malicious indicators (obfuscated payloads, credential phishing, exploit kit structures), so it didn’t under-flag real threats.

Putting it to the test

Ben and colleagues evaluated this method across three structurally different data types:

  • Command lines: ~10,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: LOLBin abuse, obfuscated PowerShell, encoded payloads.
  • HTML files: ~1,000,000 monthly ingest. Attack surface: exploit kits, credential phishing, obfuscated JavaScript.
  • RTF documents: ~10,000 monthly ingest (testing under data scarcity). Attack surface: Equation Editor exploits, DDE attacks, malicious OLE.

The results on LOLBins can be found in the previous research. But expanding the work to HTML and RTF files elucidated more generalizable trends, and suggests that the method can work with a variety of data types.

Like LOLBins, RTF performed best with isolation forest, showing a 2.41% increase over the existing model, which is an encouraging jump at such a high ROC AUC.

The baseline performance of the model is higher, so the increase is more modest, but the team found that K-means was the most effective with a 0.68% increase over baseline. They also noted that PCA decreased the score, which highlights exactly why they used three different anomaly detection methods: they didn’t know in advance which method would capture the most valuable anomalies in a particular dataset. And since running these algorithms is relatively cheap, the small extra cost only comes from running the evaluations on the extra anomalies with the LLM.

Try it yourself

Here’s something our data science-minded readers can try out for themselves:

  • Pick a file type where your classifier has a false positive or false negative problem
  • Pull a sample of unlabeled production data, featurize it, and run Isolation Forest (it's 10 lines of sklearn)
  • Send the top anomalies to an LLM with a format-specific prompt. Use two prompts: one that errs malicious, one that errs benign
  • (Optional) Check the quality of the LLM output on a sample either by running it on a set of your labeled data or even better, have an analyst verify the unlabeled ones
  • Add the high-precision labels to your next training run and measure the difference
  • Wrap it in a YAML config and schedule it. All being well, you now have a self-improving data pipeline

Top takeaways

  • Classifiers’ failure cases are a training data diversity problem; anomaly detection finds the unusual files that rules and manual labeling miss
  • Multi-method anomaly detection (IF + KMeans + PCA) on different feature representations catches more than any single method
  • Dual-prompt LLM labeling achieves high precision on both malicious and benign labels, making both usable as training data
  • The pipeline is filetype-agnostic (as long as an LLM can produce high precision labels for them – test this empirically first) and runs on a single machine. A new data type therefore requires a config file, rather than having to become an onerous engineering project
  • Although research on traditional ML models has slowed in recent times, this research shows that LLMs can help revitalize the field by infusing them into the process for significant performance gains

item.title: Malicious ScreenConnect deployments observed
item.description:
Sophos researchers are investigating an active campaign of malicious activity involving unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments. ConnectWise released an advisory confirming the incident and is investigating multiple third-party extensions possibly linked to the activity. The advisory recommends disabling the identified extensions as a precautionary measure.

In one case observed by Sophos researchers, curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185[.]99[.]255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi. A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4.

The observed malicious activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs: d905b2b1b165d0a9, 4b8f4089ddaac6a9, and df1f7ef0cfacd0d8. These are likely compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy the malicious instances. The IDs of those malicious instances are 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091. 

Recommended actions

Organizations using ScreenConnect should follow the advice in the ConnectWise advisory. To identify malicious activity, review ScreenConnect command history for unexpected client deployments or remote commands. Usage of curl and PowerShell activity that downloads ScreenConnect installers or scripts from Windows Temp, followed by msiexec.exe installation, should also be investigated. 

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs is investigating the applicability of existing countermeasures and the feasibility of developing additional countermeasures to detect activity associated with this threat. Activity is being reviewed across customer environments and will be escalated where identified.

item.title: The day the FAA halted departures nationwide
item.description:
On Friday afternoon, November 13, 2026, radar and communications at air traffic control centers went unstable, and shortly before 4 p.m. Eastern the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop. Aircraft already in the air were allowed to land, and the stop lasted more than four hours, with some exceptions, before it was lifted at 8:15 p.m. By the end of the day, thousands of flights had been canceled in what Reuters described as only the second nationwide departure stop since September 11, 2001. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy explained it that night with the plainness of someone reading off a whiteboard: "Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down. And I shouldn't say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down."

The ground stop capped a week that was already heavy with change. Microsoft's November release lists fixes for 1,094 of its own CVEs compared to 63 in November 2025. On Thursday, Exchange Online began failing. Microsoft's preliminary account now says traffic shifts during network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug, causing connection requests to queue until servers exhausted their processing capacity. Microsoft restored service gradually, validating stability at each stage. Both investigations remain preliminary, and both have said they see no evidence of an attack or AI involvement.

The week raises a familiar question: can defenders absorb a growing volume of fixes without increasing change risk? Extra approval layers can lengthen the queue without improving stability, while larger bundles can make faults harder to isolate and contain. A decade of software delivery research points to a different answer: ship smaller changes more often, roll each one out in rings sized to how varied the machines are, and give exploited flaws and other immediately exploitable, high-impact exposures priority in the fast lane.

Bigger haystacks, a smaller exploited fraction

Of the roughly 1,100 Microsoft CVEs in the November release, exactly one was flagged as exploited in the wild at release, and it wasn't one of the 63 rated critical. That one, CVE-2026-124194, is a moderate-rated Outlook flaw that can leak the user's NTLMv2 authentication hash when the user opens a specially crafted message file, potentially enabling impersonation or password cracking.

Satnam Narang of Tenable summed up the month: "For most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle." The volume is real, but the observed exploited fraction is tiny. Google's threat intelligence group observed active exploitation of only 0.23% of vulnerabilities disclosed in 2026 through August. Prioritizing an exploited vulnerability often means accelerating a package of fixes. A cumulative Windows update bundles many fixes together, so administrators stage the package containing the urgent fix across representative groups of machines. Microsoft's validation before release and an organization's testing against its own hardware and applications provide complementary checks as deployment expands.

The small exploited fraction helps explain where to concentrate effort. How quickly attackers move helps determine how urgently those fixes need to reach exposed systems. Sophos's AI Security 2026 report described CVE-2026-10520 in Ivanti Sentry exploited within 24 hours of a public proof of concept. For CVE-2026-42208 in LiteLLM, Sysdig observed exploitation attempts about 36 hours after the advisory entered GitHub's global database. CISA's June 2026 Binding Operational Directive 26-04 gave federal civilian agencies 180 days to implement risk-based remediation deadlines as short as three calendar days, citing AI as a factor that may narrow the response window. A small share of the haystack can demand a fast response, which is why the highest-risk fixes need an accelerated, monitored rollout.

Speed and stability move together

The instinct when the queue grows is to slow down and add approvals, but software delivery research shows that speed need not come at the expense of stability. Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, and Gene Kim's Accelerate, built on four years of State of DevOps surveys, found "no tradeoff between improving performance and achieving higher levels of stability and quality," and it found approval by a change advisory board had "no correlation with change fail rate." In the 2017 data, high performers deployed 46 times more often than low performers, and their changes were one-fifth as likely to fail. The book uses deployment frequency as a stand-in for smaller batches. Google's DORA program, which grew out of that research, said it again in its 2025 report, calling the speed-versus-stability trade-off "a myth" and finding that the teams strong at both made up nearly 40% of its sample.

AI enters this picture as volume. DORA's 2024 survey associated a 25% increase in AI adoption with a 7.2% drop in delivery stability, and the 2025 report associated higher AI adoption with higher delivery throughput and continued instability, with "no evidence" that AI softens the damage instability does. The surveys are observational, so they show association rather than cause. DORA's proposed explanation is that AI can enlarge changes and accelerate code production without a matching improvement in review, testing, and deployment. Forsgren and Abi Noda describe the same shift in Frictionless: when developers can generate code in minutes but deployments take hours, "the constraint shifts from creation to validation and delivery."

Outages live where changes activate

Google Cloud's June 2025 outage shows three steps that the label "bad update" hides. A release adds a defect, a later configuration change switches it on, and automation spreads it everywhere. On May 29, 2025, Google Cloud rolled out new quota-checking code region by region, exactly as careful operators do, but the failing code path was not exercised during that rollout. On June 12, a routine policy update with some fields left blank copied itself to every region within seconds and triggered that code path. The code lacked a feature flag for staged activation and appropriate handling for missing values, so the service that approves Google Cloud API requests crashed and restarted in a loop everywhere at once. A change that switches on everywhere at once is the largest batch there is, however small the diff.

Cloudflare encountered a similar problem in December 2025 while expanding request-body inspection to protect customers against a newly disclosed vulnerability. That change was rolling out gradually. When an internal testing tool proved incompatible with the larger buffer, engineers disabled it through a separate configuration system that propagated globally within seconds. Turning the tool off triggered errors in part of Cloudflare’s proxy fleet. The main rollout was staged, but the supporting configuration change was not.

The controls around a release need the same discipline as the release itself. Turning a feature off, changing a flag, or retiring an old code path can change production behavior. Those operations need testing and containment too. Temporary rollout flags should be deliberately retired once their job is done, while retained recovery switches need owners and tested behavior.

Small, frequent changes are easier when the operator controls the rollout and rollback path, though even a cloud fleet has varied hardware and configurations. Microsoft's Azure team, which has called change the primary cause of its reliability problems other than routine hardware failures, normally rolls changes through canary and pilot stages, waiting at each stage while it watches health signals. Distributed fleets are harder, because endpoints, branch sites, and air traffic control centers run different hardware, drivers, and configurations, and a bad change can knock out the very connection that would deliver the fix. There the early rings carry the load, because they're the first place a change meets machines nobody could test on.

Blocking both sites stabilized the network, and the broadcasting function was disabled on the new routers. The initiating fault remains under investigation, and the public account does not establish what testing or isolation preceded the work.

Security content can combine a fast cadence with operating-system-level consequences. The file was released without staged rollout and was live for 78 minutes before CrowdStrike pulled it. Microsoft estimated 8.5 million Windows devices were affected. The bad content was withdrawn quickly, but restoring affected machines was a separate job, involving manual remediation guidance, scripts, and automated recovery efforts.

Monthly code and driver updates, which can reach the kernel, spend weeks in stabilization and then move through rings that start with Microsoft's "hundreds of thousands of employees and millions of internal devices," watched for reliability, performance, and compatibility "across hardware and software configurations." Detection updates ship several times a day, too often for that process, so Microsoft keeps kernel changes out of them entirely, still stages them from internal devices to early-access customers before everyone else, and says it can mitigate problems "through the cloud in minutes." Content that only touches user-mode components and can be pulled back from the cloud can ship several times a day, while content parsed by kernel-mode code, like Crowdstrike’s Channel File 291, can fail with operating-system-level consequences. item.title: Sophos Endpoint adds boot-time driver protection built on the Windows endpoint security platform
item.description:
Attackers are moving faster. As the Sophos Exploits Explained whitepaper shows, AI is making it quicker and easier for adversaries to discover vulnerabilities and turn them into working exploits. When attacks move this quickly, there isn’t always time to wait for a person to step in. The laptop, desktop, or server under attack often must stop it on its own. That makes protection on the device a critical line of defense, and it’s why endpoint protection is a top priority at Sophos.

To stop the most dangerous attacks, you need to see what Windows does at its deepest level, starting the moment a device turns on. Drivers are among the most trusted software on a Windows device. Many run at the core of the operating system, and some start before almost anything else, which attackers know well. Malware that poses as a driver can take hold before most security software even starts. Sophos Endpoint already blocks known malicious drivers as Windows starts, using an integration with the Early Launch Antimalware (ELAM) security feature.

How Sophos handles deep access to Windows

Sophos invests heavily in ensuring the appropriate level of access to Windows to protect against the adversary. Our engineers work at the lowest levels of the operating system, where one mistake can affect the whole device, not just a single app. So we test every change thoroughly, release updates in stages, and watch closely as they roll out. We want strong protection that doesn’t get in the way of the people who rely on those devices to do their jobs.

New: boot-time driver protection on the Windows endpoint security platform

The Windows endpoint security platform from Microsoft gives security companies a way to get deep visibility and control while reducing reliance on kernel-mode code. Security products can now watch for threats and act on them from user mode, the same space where everyday applications run, instead of placing more of their own code at the core of Windows. With less security code at the core, a failure is less likely to affect the whole device. Microsoft also built in recovery. If a security product or protection rule causes a problem during startup, Windows includes recovery mechanisms designed to restore the system.

Today, we’re announcing the first Sophos integration with the platform. Starting in the fourth quarter of 2026, we extend the existing boot-time protection for customers running Windows 11 to block malicious or untrusted drivers as Windows starts, using Sophos technology built on the Windows endpoint security platform. Sophos identifies each driver by a unique digital fingerprint of the file, so renaming a driver won’t let it slip through. Customers get boot-time protection on a platform designed to keep devices stable.

“Deep access to Windows provides defenders with a meaningful advantage. Our engineers have spent years mastering how Windows works at its core so we can stop attackers at the earliest possible moment. Every protection we ship must do two things: stop the threat and keep our customers’ businesses running. Boot-time driver protection on the Windows endpoint security platform does both. It strengthens protection at startup and reduces the risk that a security update ever disrupts a customer’s device.”

– John Peterson, CTO, Sophos

Turning it on

Customers decide when and where to turn it on. Customers can switch to the new method or stay with the startup protection they rely on today.

Sophos Fusion logs every startup block, so teams have a record when something needs a closer look. Endpoint Self Help, the Sophos Endpoint troubleshooting tool, shows the installed driver version and the policy settings in use. A good way to start is with a small group of devices. Check the results, then roll it out more widely.

Working with Microsoft

Sophos has worked closely with Microsoft on the platform since the Windows Endpoint Security Ecosystem Summit in September 2024, where Microsoft and security partners agreed on a shared goal of making Windows more reliable without weakening security. Sophos engineers helped shape the platform by sharing what we see while protecting more than 300,000+ organizations that use Sophos Endpoint. 

The latest Sophos Endpoint release also includes drivers certified and signed by Microsoft through the Windows Hardware Compatibility Program (WHCP). That signature confirms the drivers passed the program’s compatibility tests and lets Windows verify that Sophos published them and no one has changed them.

This work builds on a long-standing relationship, including Sophos integrations with Microsoft Graph, which bring Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Defender alerts into Sophos XDR and Sophos MDR, and Sophos membership in the Microsoft Intelligent Security Association (MISA) and the Microsoft Virus Initiative (MVI).

Protection that keeps pace

Attacks are likely to keep getting faster as AI improves, so protection needs to start on the device, and early. We’ll keep investing in deep, responsible access to Windows, so customers get stronger protection and devices that stay up and running.

To learn more about Sophos Endpoint, visit sophos.com/endpoint.

item.title: Hijacked Optimizely snippets served malicious code on major websites
item.description:
On November 17, 2026, Optimizely reported that an attacker exploited a vulnerability in its Web Experimentation product to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. Third-party reporting indicates that the code was injected into snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC, and Zoom, on November 16. Optimizely says it has fixed the vulnerability and removed the code.

Recommended actions

Sophos X-Ops recommends that organizations monitor the Optimizely incident page to stay up to date on the latest recommendations.

Sophos countermeasures

The following Sophos countermeasure relates to this threat:

  • Troj/JSInj-H

item.title: 'Java4Shell' vulnerability (CVE-2026-114938) could allow remote code execution
item.description:
On November 17, 2026, Oracle released updates to address multiple vulnerabilities in Java SE, including an issue in the Base64 decoder. This memory corruption vulnerability (CVE-2026-114938) has been dubbed “Java4Shell” and assigned a high-severity CVSS score of 8.1. The issue exists in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM in the Java Development Kit (JDK). Successful exploitation using crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM or lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. 

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued an alert on November 17 urging organizations to patch immediately. No active exploitation has been reported as of this publication.

Recommended actions

Organizations should identify vulnerable Java runtimes and apply the November 2026 Oracle Java SE updates as appropriate. Internet-facing x86-64 services that decode untrusted Base64 input should be prioritized.

Oracle’s general workaround guidance for the November 2026 update is to block the network protocols an attack requires until patches are applied. Oracle lists the protocol for CVE-2026-114938 as “Multiple” and warns that this workaround may break application functionality.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs is investigating the applicability of existing countermeasures and the feasibility of developing additional countermeasures to detect activity associated with this threat. Activity is being reviewed across customer environments and will be escalated where identified.

An internal investigation is also underway to determine if Sophos products or services are affected.

item.title: Patches released for critical ‘NGINX2Root’ vulnerabilities
item.description:
On November 18, 2026, F5 published security advisories for five critical (CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2) vulnerabilities that Xint has collectively dubbed ‘NGINX2Root’: (K000163925, K000163926, K000163927, K000163928, and K000163931). The issues affect NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus configurations. Exploitation could lead to crashes, denial of service, memory corruption, or code execution. According to F5, code execution requires ASLR to be disabled or bypassed.

Two of the vulnerabilities relate to NGINX HTTP/2 handling, and Wiz Research reports that they can be used to bypass Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR):

  • CVE-2026-123007 is an integer underflow issue in HTTP/2 flow control 
  • CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free issue affecting HTTP/2 connections that are proxied to a backend 

The other three issues are use-after-free flaws that require specific configurations:

  • CVE-2026-123634 affects the NGINX resolver in some NGINX Open Source versions when NGINX proxies to a server name that contains variables and an SSI or mirror directive sends a subrequest that resolves the same name
  • CVE-2026-121810 affects HTTP/3 configurations in some NGINX Open Source versions
  • CVE-2026-113425 affects some NGINX Open Source versions when configured as a mail proxy server

Xint reports that each vulnerability can be chained with a separate Linux kernel SCTP vulnerability to obtain root privileges on the host, including when NGINX runs in a Docker container. 

Recommended actions

Organizations should review the F5 advisories and upgrade vulnerable versions as appropriate. Updated source code and Linux packages for NGINX Open Source are also available from the NGINX website. Packages may not be immediately available for older, unsupported distributions. Xint notes that nginx -s reload does not load the new binary, so NGINX must be restarted or its binary upgraded after updating. If immediate upgrades are not possible, F5 advises avoiding SSI or mirror directives and proxied server names with variables (CVE-2026-123634), and restricting mail proxy listeners to trusted networks (CVE-2026-113425). For the HTTP/2 flaws, Wiz and Xint recommend disabling HTTP/2 on affected listeners but note that there may be implications for that action. 

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this vulnerability and will deliver detections and protections as available.

An internal investigation is also underway to determine if Sophos products or services are affected.

item.title: Every Detail Matters: From DFIR Intake to Investigative Context
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.


A security team notices unusual activity involving a user account. There are suspicious authentication events and unexpected mailbox activity.  By the time the organization reaches out for Digital Forensics and Incident Response support, several actions have already been taken. The user's password has been reset, active sessions have been revoked, and a suspicious mailbox rule has been removed. 

At first, the situation may appear relatively straightforward. An account was compromised, the immediate security concern has been addressed, and the organization now wants to understand what happened.  But as the initial conversation with the DFIR First Responder begins, the picture often becomes more complicated. 

The first version of the incident story 

The affected organization begins by walking the First Responder through what they observed and when they observed it. The suspicious mailbox activity may have been discovered only recently, but an unusual authentication event occurred several days earlier. A security alert appeared around the same period, although it did not initially seem connected. Another change may have been identified on the affected account before the wider incident was recognized. 

Individually, these details may seem insignificant. Together, they begin to establish something much more useful: the first version of the incident timeline. 

This is an important part of the First Responder conversation that can easily be overlooked. The First Responder is not performing the forensic investigation during the initial scoping conversation. Instead, the purpose is to capture the organization's understanding of the incident while the sequence of events is still relatively fresh. 

The discussion establishes when the unusual activity was first noticed, what triggered the escalation, which users, identities, or systems appeared to be involved, what actions had already been taken, what business impact had been experienced, and what security telemetry or other information might still be available. 

Not everything discussed during that conversation will ultimately prove relevant, and not every assumption will turn out to be correct. That is expected. At this stage, the value comes from capturing the context that can help the Incident Commander and investigators know where to begin. 

Small details can change the investigation 

One of the challenges with cyber incidents is that the significance of an individual event is not always obvious when it first occurs. An authentication alert two days before the discovery of suspicious mailbox activity might initially appear unrelated. Later, when investigators reconstruct identity activity, that same alert could help establish an earlier point in the incident timeline. 

The actions taken by the organization can be equally important. A password reset may explain why suspicious authentication suddenly stopped. A firewall change may explain a break in network communication. A server reboot may help investigators understand why certain volatile artifacts are no longer available. An endpoint isolation event may establish precisely when communication between systems ended. 

During that first conversation, these are not treated as forensic conclusions. They are pieces of context that may become important as investigators compare the organization's account of events with endpoint telemetry, identity logs, cloud audit records, email activity, network data, and other available evidence. 

Sometimes the evidence confirms what the organization initially believed. Sometimes it reveals that the activity began earlier, extended further, or followed a different path altogether. That is where the initial conversation starts to show its real value. 

Two sides of the same incident 

Every cyber incident has a story from the organization's perspective. They know when users began reporting problems, when an alert appeared, which systems seemed affected, and what their security and IT teams did in response. The forensic evidence provides another perspective. 

Investigators can use that evidence to determine whether suspicious activity began earlier than initially believed, whether additional identities or systems were involved, and whether seemingly unrelated events were actually part of the same sequence. 

Initial description: “We identified suspicious mailbox activity and reset the affected account.” 

After the First Responder call: Suspicious mailbox activity was discovered, but authentication anomalies had occurred earlier, and several response actions were taken before escalation, including a credential reset, session revocation, and removal of a suspicious mailbox rule. Authentication and audit records may therefore help reconstruct what happened before those actions were taken. 

The second description still does not tell investigators exactly what happened. What it provides is something equally important at this stage: a better place to start. 

In practice, this means an incident often has two timelines developing in parallel. One represents the activity that occurred within the environment. The other records how the organization discovered and responded to that activity. The First Responder begins connecting those two perspectives. 

If suspicious activity stops at a particular time, for example, knowing that the organization revoked active sessions moments earlier gives investigators important context. Without that information, the same evidence could tell a very different story. 

More than estimating the effort 

It can be easy to think of a DFIR scoping call primarily as a way to understand the size of an incident, establish the required expertise, and estimate the response effort. Those are important outcomes, but the value of the First Responder conversation goes further. 

A well-structured First Responder conversation captures the organization's first-hand account while the events surrounding the incident are still fresh. It begins separating what is known from what is suspected, establishes what has already changed since discovery, identifies potential sources of evidence, and surfaces the questions that matter most to the people living through the incident. 

By the time the Incident Commander and forensic investigators begin their work, they are not simply starting with a statement such as “the organization reported a compromised account.” They have an initial picture of what the organization experienced, what was observed, what actions were taken, when those actions occurred, and where potentially useful evidence may exist. 

The First Responder does not provide the forensic answer. Instead, they capture the context that helps investigators know where to begin looking for that answer. 

Where the investigation really begins 

Digital forensic investigations are ultimately driven by evidence. Endpoint artifacts, identity activity, network telemetry, email records, cloud audit logs, and other sources help investigators reconstruct what actually occurred. But evidence rarely arrives with the surrounding story already attached. 

That context often begins with the people closest to the incident. The First Responder captures the initial account and begins organizing the fragments into a coherent incident picture. The Incident Commander and investigators can then validate, challenge, and expand that picture using the available forensic evidence. 

Sometimes the investigation confirms the organization's initial understanding. Sometimes it shows that the incident started earlier than anyone realized. Events that originally appeared unrelated may turn out to be connected. In other cases, the evidence may reveal a completely different sequence of events. 

That ability to move from an initial understanding to an evidence-supported account of what happened is one of the things that makes digital forensics so valuable. 

For the organization on the other end of the line, the initial DFIR call may simply feel like the first conversation after asking for help. Behind that conversation, however, something important is already happening. The timeline is beginning to take shape. Actions already performed are being documented. Potential sources of evidence are being identified. Known facts are beginning to separate from assumptions, and the questions that may guide the investigation are becoming clearer. 

That is why the First Responder conversation is more than estimating the potential size or effort of an incident response engagement. 

It captures the first version of the incident story. 

The forensic investigation may confirm that story, expand it, or completely rewrite it, but before investigators can establish what really happened, they need a meaningful place to start.  Quite often, that starting point is the conversation that happened before the investigation even began.
